The abundant opaque minerals appear to be primary; corro­ sion rims are absent; leucoxene, though present, is not abundant. Fine-grained secondary hematite is seen pen­ etrating along cracks. The intermediate rocks are bluish in hand sample. In thin section they appear to be predominantly andesitic. As in the case of the basic rocks, the felspar and fer­ romagnesian minerals are largely chloritized and sericitized, and the association of this with chlorite, sphene and epidote suggests the dikes have been sub­ jected to low-grade metamorphism and altered hydro­ thermally. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: No deviations were noted when compared with orienting with the compass more distant from the dike. They were sliced to a standard length in the laboratory, most commonly giving one core per sample. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the cores was measured using a "Digico complete results magnetometer" interfaced with a Digital MINC com­ puter. There was a considerable range in the intensity of NRM ranging from values of 8 x 104 ntAm"! to about 1.3 x 108 rrtAm"! in the basic dikes, to a maximum of 1.5 x 10- 4 mAm"! in the intermediate dikes, down to 1 x 10-3 to 3 X 10- 1 rrtAm"! in the acidic rocks. Pro­ gressive alternating field demagnetization of the natural remanent magnetization in a Schonstedt GSD-1 was carried out in 5 mTsteps to 25 mT, above that at 35, 50, 75 and 100 mT on two pilot cores per site (Fig. 3). Thermal demagnetization using the Schonstedt TD was carried out on some samples. The first stages of heating were generally at widely spaced intervals begin­ ning at 200°C and then at 100°C steps, but as higher temperatures were reached the interval was reduced to 50°C (Fig. 4). Programs available on the MINC allowed us to calcu­ late the usual statistical parameters and to compute the vector of the magnetization removed between progres­ sive demagnetization steps. This proved necessary in some samples which have superposed magnetic vectors.

DISCUSSION OF RESULTS (1) Directions of remanence The measurements of the direction of remanence during progressive demagnetization permit us to distin­ guish three patterns of behaviour. For most of the acid and basic dikes examined, and about half of the ande­ sites, after the elimination of a small viscous component there appeared to be but a single component, for the direction of magnetization remained virtually unchanged during demagnetization. This behaviour is illustrated through stable end point curves (Figs 5 and 6) and is the same whether alternating field or thermal techniques were applied. These curves also illustrate the point that in some samples the directions of magnetiza­ tion do not always decay exactly toward the origin, although the directions of magnetization are identical to those of other samples from the same site which do. In some cases an improvement occurred when thermal treatment was applied to samples demagnetized in alter­ nating fields (BM 372, Fig. 7). They extend for about 75 km from south of Ras Gharib to just north of Hurghada (Fig. 1) and at their broadest point are just over 6 km wide. The range rises above the coastal plain to the east, and to the west is separated by a wide valley from the main mass of the Red Sea Hills. Both areas are covered by recent sedi­

Although most of this shield is mantled by younger sediments, there are extensive out- crops of the basement rocks in Egypt on both sides of the Gulf of Suez. The outcrops in the Red Sea Hills have been known since the pioneer work of Hume (1934) and others, although with a few notable exceptions little detailed mapping or modern geophysical/geochemical surveying has been carried out. The general strati- graphy, however, has been outlined on several occa- sions, and Table 1 provides one of the more recent of such summaries. The older rocks of the basement complex are com- monly metamorphosed to amphibolite facies; however, the rocks of the younger formations (the Dokhan Vol- canic Formation, the Hammamat Group and the Younger Granites) are not only less metamorphosed, but are lithologically suitable for paleomagnetic investi- gation. Azimuthal orientation was made in the field by magnetic compass. The open end of the plastic cube was aligned parallel to the vertical face of the outcrop and samples were taken at 10 cm intervals. Five pilot specimens from the Teleki Valley site and 12 from the Hobley Valley site were selected and these were subjected to stepwise alternating field (a.f.) demagnetization at levels of 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50 and 60 miUitesla (mT) in a conventional three-axis tumbler. On the basis of this information, and the reversely mag- netized till found in Hobley Valley an age of approxi- mately 730,000 yr B.P. or greater can be assigned to the oldest tills found on Mount Kenya. The magnetic record for HOB19 may mark the Brunhes/Matuyama border (0.73 m.y.) or one of the magnetic events within the Matuyama Chron. Ages of 0.9 and 0.97 m.y. for the Jaramillo, 1.87 m.y. for the Olduvai and 2.04 and 2.12 m.y. for the R6union are also likely candidates in that they mark polarity transitions from a reversed to a normal field with decreasing time during the Pleistocene. Abstract- Results of a palaeomagnetic study carried out on the Migori granites exposed in the South Western part of Kenya are presented. The granites of Post-Nyanzian and Post- Kaviron- dian ages are dated at 2739 5:111 Ma and 2420 5:60 Ma, respectively, using the whole rock Rb- Sr isochron method. Alternating frequency and thermal demagnetization techniques have been used to isolate characteristic components of natural remanence. Opaque petrological and thermomagnetic studies indicate titanomagnetite grains as the main carrier of the primary component. The low paleolatitude of the Lawrence Head Volcanics supports the location of a major Ordovician subduction system near the Laurentian margin of Iapetus, whereas the present-day juxtaposition of latitudinally distinct elements in the area represents a complex accretionary history involving Early Silurian or older thrusting and younger strike-slip faulting of several Iapetan island-arc terranes to Laurentia. 1. MCRAE2 Department of Earth Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire 03755 ABSTRACT Fine-scaled stratigraphic data are combined with chronologic information provided by paleomagnetic stratigraphy to document and analyze chronostratigraphic variability of the Salla Beds, a sequence of distal floodplain and lacustrine intermontane basin sediments within the eastern Andean cordillera of Bolivia. Unsteadiness in sediment accumulation is identified using a conceptual model of episodic accumulation in which simulated accumulation histories are constructed using estimated rates for various fluvial facies and taking into account gaps in deposition and possible effects of erosion. Over longer time inter- vals these controls interact to produce the pattern of sediment accumulation in a partic- ular depositional system. Using paleomagnetic isochrons, this inves- tigation, and the companion study (McRae 1990), present two examples that identify chronostratigraphic variability in fluvial stratigraphic sequences at various levels of resolution. The analysis of high-resolution sedimentologic and chronologic data from the Lower Chinji Formation on the Potwar Plateau of northern Pakistan (McRae 1990) documents patterns of unsteadiness and non- uniformity of sediment accumulation in the floodplain environment of a large, through- going river system in the foreland basin along the southern margin of the Himalayan colli- s'ional orogen. The present paper (1) de- scribes the physical stratigraphy and associ- ated sedimentiology of the Salla Beds, a sequence of distal floodplain and lacustrine intermontane basin sediments situated within the eastern Andean Cordillera of Bolivia; (2) documents and analyzes, in a manner similar to that in the companion study, the chrono- str

cumulation in terrestrial basins. PHYSICAL STRATIGRAPHY AND SEDIMENTOLOGY Regional Geologic Framework.-The Salla-Luribay Basin is situated within the eastern Andean Cordillera, near the eastern margin of the Altiplano, a major intermon- tane plateau (elevation above 3800 m) that extends north-south from Peru to Argentina. The basin is bounded by deformed and lo- cally metamorphosed Paleozoic sediments (Martinez and Tomasi 1978; Lavenu 1986) and is one of several small intermontane ba- sins on the margins of the Altiplano where significant thicknesses of non-marine Ter- tiary sediments are exposed. The Salla de- posits are the site of a diverse suite of ex- tinct fossil vertebrates that have been exten- sively collected by Bolivian, French, and North American paleontologists since the mid 1960s. THE RIO AZUL SECTION Three fault zones are recognized in the Rio Azul section whose offsets are large enough that units cannot be matched across the fault at the scale of single outcrops; these zones occur at 490, 865, and 960 m above the base of the Neogene section. Geochronology.-Samples for radioiso- topic dating were collected from two tufface- ous horizons interbedded within our mea- sured sections at Quebrada Honda. The lower sample, QH-9, occurs 82 m above the base of our measured section 1 (fig. 4). The upper sample, QH-17, comes from the 255 m level within our measured section 2 (fig. 4). These samples were analyzed using the 40K/40Ar method at the geochronology labora- tory at the Australian National University. After crushing and then washing to remove fine-grained material, these ash samples were processed using standard mineral separation techniques, i.e., a combination of heavy liq- uid and magnetic separation, and seiving. Final separates were thoroughly sonified in acetone to remove any traces of organic sol- vents. Sample QH-9 sanidine contained several percent cloudy grains. The sample was treated in an ultrasonic bath for 3 min, fol- lowed by additional magnetic separation. This entire procedure yielded an essentially pure separate (>99.9%) of clear grains. There remained, however, a few grains containing inclusions. Both biotite samples QH-9 and QH-17 appeared very fresh and consisted of >99.9% pure biotite. The analytical data for these

a few grains containing inclusions. Both biotite samples QH-9 and QH-17 appeared very fresh and consisted of >99.9% pure biotite. The analytical data for these samples are presented in table 2. Ar concentrations were determined by isotope dilution using an 38Ar spike having a concentration known to better than 0.75%. The interpretation of conventional 4oK/4Ar results obtained from young air-fall volcan- ics, although straightforward in terms of Ar systematics, must take into account several possible sources of geological error. Biotite ages can be incorrect as a result of weath- ering, and both sanidine and biotite ages can be anomalously old due to detrital contamina- tion. This locality is constrained by a fission-track age determination of 6.9 ± 1.1 Ma, and the local magnetostratigraphy is correlated to Chron 7 on the MPTS. The fossil mammals from this section have an extrapolated age of about 7.3 to 7.4 Ma. In conjunction with two other published data sets (Ocros, 130 S, and Salla, 170 S), these late Tertiary Andean localities indicate counterclockwise rotation at 130 S, negligible rotation at 170 S, and clockwise rotation at 22° S. These data could represent local small-block rotations on a scale greater than about 6 km2. However, these data are also consistent with a model of late Neogene bending of the Bolivian Orocline.

(1) Quebrada Honda, located at 22° S lat., consists of a 300 m thick section containing abundant Santacrucian or Friasian (middle Miocene) fossil mammals. This locality is constrained by mean 40K/40Ar ages of 12.83 ± 0.11 Ma and 11.96 ± 0.11 Ma, and the local magnetostratigraphy is correlated to chrons C5AA through C5A on the Magnetic Polarity Time Scale (MPTS). The fossil mammals from Quebrada Honda have an extrapolated age of about 13.0 to 12.7 Ma. (2) Micafia, located at 170 S lat., consists of a 205 m thick section containing late Miocene fossil mammals, including a megatheriid sloth and the tiny mesothere Microtypotherium cf. M. choquecotense. This locality is constrained by a fission-track age determination of 6.9 ± 1.1 Ma, and the local magnetostratigraphy is correlated to Chron 7 on the MPTS. The fossil mammals from this section have an extrapolated age of about 7.3 to 7.4 Ma. In conjunction with two other published data sets (Ocros, 130 S, and Salla, 170 S), t

ret a local magnetostratigraphy, thereby resulting in usable data from 87% of the originally sampled sites. These data re- sulted in a local magnetostratigraphy consist- ing of 14 magnetozones, R1-N7 (fig. 5). The local correlation between the Que- brada Honda and Rio Rosario sections, which are separated by about 6 km, is difficult because of several factors including: (1) the lack of demonstrable lateral continuity of persistent units, like the tuffaceous hori- zons; (2) significant facies changes between sections; (3) radiometric calibrations only available for Quebrada Honda; and (4) the fact that the magnetic polarity time scale is very "busy" during the Miocene, thereby re- sulting in numerous small polarity events. Dating Results.-A total of 367 single- crystal feldspar analyses were obtained from 20 samples collected from the three measured stratigraphic sections (table 2). Radiogenic argon (40Ar*) constituted >85% of the argon released during fusion of all but eight grains. These less radiogenic feldspars were ex- cluded from subsequent analysis because of the possibility of alteration. Individual anal- yses typically yielded age uncertainties be- tween 0.03 and 0.06 m.y. (0.2 to 0.4%). The 40Ar/39Ar analyses are plotted as age histograms in figure 2. Six samples exhibit unimodal, near-symmetrical age distributions without outliers, nine display prominent pri- mary peaks with tails of older ages, while five show either poorly populated associations of young ages (RD-52, 31/1/84A) or scattered distributions without dominant components (RD-22, 1/2/84B, and 28/1/84A). Unimodal, near-symmetric distributions of feldspar ages within a volcaniclastic deposit suggest origi- nation from an eruptive event that rapidly saturated the depositional environment with juvenile pyroclastic material. These ages range from 13.06 Ma at the base to 10.51 Ma toward the top of the type section near Kabarsero. Correlation of the local paleomagnetic stratigraphies with the geomagnetic reversal time scale yields magnetochronologic

ntation rates at Kabarsero calculated from the 40Ar/39Ar results decrease from initial values of -25 cm/1000 yr to -5 cm/1000 yr toward the top of the section. The initial rapid sedimentation rates characterize the first 0.1 to 0.3 m.y. following emplacement of the underlying, voluminous, basin-filling Tiim Phonolites, indicating that the Baringo Basin at this time may not have existed as a rift valley created by extensional tectonics, but instead may have been a subsidence feature formed in response to removal of large volumes of magma from the lithosphere. A premolar tentatively identified as Proconsul sp. indet. found in the Ngorora Formation near the village of Bartabwa has been dated at --12.42 Ma, representing perhaps the last known occurrence of this genus in the fossil record. The corresponding paleomagnetic pole at 52.4°N 111.0°E is similar to those of the remagnetized carbonates in Ontario and New York State, suggesting that the Michigan formations were also remagnetized in the late Paleozoic. Rock magnetic characterizations suggest that the characteristic magnetization is carried by single and pseudosingle domain magnetite grains. Very fine rounded single crystal magnetite grains, believed to be products of chemical precipitation, observed by scanning and scanning transmission electron micro- scope (SEM/STEM) are inferred to be the carrier of the remagnetization. Paired carbon isotope analyses of bulk carbonate and anhysteretic susceptibility (Xarm) of cuttings from two wells were examined to test the hypothesis that oxidation of hydrocarbons may lead to formation of authigenic magnetite. Oil saturated horizons and overlying strata in a producing well exhibit lower Xarm intensities than the equivalent horizons in an adjacent non-producing well.

Oil saturated horizons and overlying strata in a producing well exhibit lower Xarm intensities than the equivalent horizons in an adjacent non-producing well. Little correlation between Xam and 613C is observed in carbonate-rich lithologies due to the masking of the hydrocarbon related cement compositions by the host carbonate. In contrast, carbonate-poor shale horizons overlying hydrocarbon-rich strata in the producing well exhibit strong correlative peaks in Xarm and 6S3C. The overall lower Xarm intensities in the hydrocarbon-producing well suggest that it is not merely the presence of hydrocarbons which promotes authigenic magnetite formation. Rather, the magnetite/hydrocarbon relationship more likely records pro- cesses associated with hydrocarbon migration and interaction with oxidizing subsurface fluids in areas peripheral to sites of accumulation. Scipio and Stoney Point fields (figure 1). Five wells, Conklin 1-31, Casler 1-30, Casler 5-30, Figure 1. Symbols are solid circle, producing well; half-solid cir- cle, producing but non-profitable well; open circle, dry well; dashed line, boundary of oil/gas field; and dash- dotted line, county boundary. Tolle 1-33, and Hall 1-13, have penetrated the Trenton and Black River Formations and have pro- vided cores for our paleomagnetic, rock magnetic, and SEM/STEM investigations (figure 1). From each 2.54 cm diameter core sample, two or three standard 11.4 cm 3 specimens were cut. One specimen for each sample was devoted to the study of microfacies, while the remaining speci- mens were used for paleomagnetic and rock mag- netic analyses. The specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization. Magnetic rema- nence measurements were made with a "2G" cryo- genic magnetometer housed in a magnetically shielded room with an internal ambient field of about 200 nT. Mineral alteration during heating was monitored with a Bartington Susceptibility Meter (MS2). Magnetization components for indi- vidual specimens were picked by eye from ortho- gonal projections of thermal demagnetization data (Zijderveld, 1967). Introduction The island of Hydra (Fig. 1) is part of the Subpelagonian Zone and exhibits a well preserved Permian to Jurassic sedimentary sequence (R6mermann et al., 1981; Baud et al., 1991; Angiolini et al., 1992). Angiolini et al. (1992) reported a section with Late Illyrian (Late Anisian) conodonts outcropping near the monastery of Aghia Triada (Fig. 1 ). The section is comprised of the Han-Bulog Limestone, a red nodular facies widespread in the Tethyan Triassic. Angiolini et al. (1992) inferred the location of the Anisian- Ladinian boundary in this section on the basis of lithological correlations to other sections outcrop- ping on the island. It has been studied for its Illiryan conodonts (section H in Angiolini et al., 1992), as well as for Illyrian ammonoids (Renz, 1931). The Aghia Marina section is located in the Southern thrust sheet, near the Aghia Marina chapel (Fig. 1). It is more condensed than the Aghia Triada section, and it is composed of a few meters of Han-Bulog Lst. It corresponds to the lowermost part of section A of Angiolini et al. (1992). 3. Lithostratigraphy The Aghia Triada section is 24.6 m thick and is lithologically fairly homogeneous (Fig. 3). (I) From 0.0 to 7.2 m: centimeter-thick beds of grey to pink-grey nodular limestones alternating with red marls and nodules bounded by red matrix, rich in ammonoids, crinoids and filaments (pelagic bivalves). Calcarenites and calcareous breccia levels made up of grey to pink millimetric to centimetric limestone clasts in a red matrix with filaments are also present. (2) From 7.2 to 9.0 m: centimetre-thick planar beds of red limestones. (3) From 9.0 to 15.0 m: centimetre-thick beds of filament-bearing grey to pink-grey limestone nodules with red marly matrix. (4) From 16.0 to 24.6 m: grey limestones with

Paleomagnetic analysis Samples were collected using a portable gaso- line-powered drill and oriented by magnetic com- pass. From each 2.54 cm diameter core sample, two or three standard 11.4 cm 3 specimens were cut. One specimen for each sample was devoted to the study of microfacies, while the remaining speci- mens were used for paleomagnetic and rock mag- netic analyses. The specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization. Magnetic rema- nence measurements were made with a "2G" cryo- genic magnetometer housed in a magnetically shielded room with an internal ambient field of about 200 nT. Mineral alteration during heating was monitored with a Bartington Susceptibility Meter (MS2). Magnetization components for indi- vidual specimens were picked by eye from ortho- gonal projections of thermal demagnetization data (Zijderveld, 1967). The standard least squares method (Kirschvink, 1980) was applied to deter- mine the component directions. Section mean directions were determined using standard Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953). Lithostratigraphy The Aghia Triada section is 24.6 m thick and is lithologically fairly homogeneous (Fig. 3). (I) From 0.0 to 7.2 m: centimeter-thick beds of grey to pink-grey nodular limestones alternating with red marls and nodules bounded by red matrix, rich in ammonoids, crinoids and filaments (pelagic bivalves). Calcarenites and calcareous breccia levels made up of grey to pink millimetric to centimetric limestone clasts in a red matrix with filaments are also present. (2) From 7.2 to 9.0 m: centimetre-thick planar beds of red limestones. (3) From 9.0 to 15.0 m: centimetre-thick beds of filament-bearing grey to pink-grey limestone nodules with red marly matrix. Paleomagnetic analysis Samples were collected using a portable gaso- line-powered drill and oriented by magnetic com- pass. From each 2.54 cm diameter core sample, two or three standard 11.4 cm 3 specimens were cut. One specimen for each sample was devoted to the study of microfacies, while the remaining speci- mens were used for paleomagnetic and rock mag- netic analyses. The specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization. Magnetic rema- nence measurements were made with a "2G" cryo- genic magnetometer housed in a magnetically shielded room with an internal ambient field of about 200 nT. Mineral alteration during heating was monitored with a Bartington Susceptibility Meter (MS2). Magnetization components for indi- vidual specimens were picked by eye from ortho- gonal projections of thermal demagnetization data (Zijderveld, 1967). The standard least squares method (Kirschvink, 1980) was applied to deter- mine the component directions. Section mean directions were determined using standard Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953). From each 2.54 cm diameter core sample, two or three standard 11.4 cm 3 specimens were cut. One specimen for each sample was devoted to the study of microfacies, while the remaining speci- mens were used for paleomagnetic and rock mag- netic analyses. The specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization. Lithostratigraphy The Aghia Triada section is 24.6 m thick and is lithologically fairly homogeneous (Fig. 3). (I) From 0.0 to 7.2 m: centimeter-thick beds of grey to pink-grey nodular limestones alternating with red marls and nodules bounded by red matrix, rich in ammonoids, crinoids and filaments (pelagic bivalves). Calcarenites and calcareous breccia levels made up of grey to pink millimetric to centimetric limestone clasts in a red matrix with filaments are also present. (2) From 7.2 to 9.0 m: centimetre-thick planar beds of red limestones. (3) From 9.0 to 15.0 m: centimetre-thick beds of filament-bearing grey to pink-grey limestone nodules with red marly matrix. Their trends vary between north (to NE) and south (to SW) with variable strike lengths (0.1 to 8 kin) and widths (<1 to 15 m). At a few places, they cross-cut the dolerite dykes. The alkaline dykes are either green/grey or reddish brown in colour and consist almost entirely of alkali feldspar and alkali pyroxenes. The reddish brown dykes were described as altered dykes (Dawson and Hargraves, 1994). Dif- fusion of hematite staining and alteration of feldspars and cores of pyroxene grains is evident. The alter- ation is most likely deuteric. Ikramuddin and Stueber (1976) reported whole-rock Rb-Sr isotope data on eight samples yielding an isochron age of 832 + 40 Ma and K-Ar whole-rock age of 810 + 25 Ma for one of the dykes. Anilkumar et al., 1989 (cf. Rad- hakrishna and Mathew, 1993) reported an isochron age of 823 :t: 15 Ma based on a combined Rb-Sr isotope data of whole-rock and alkali feldspar grains of the alkaline dykes. It was deposited at "--3000 Ma and deformed by a mobile episode at ~2700 Ma. Most K-Ar ages obtained in the rim basalts range from 5 to 8 Ma (Luedke and Smith, 1978). The oldest volcanoes and lava flows of the SF volcanic field are found where they overlap the basalts along the southwest margin of the field; it is not clear whether there is a break in time between volcanism of the rim basalt and that of the SF field. Hence, the boundary of the field is ill defined on the southwest; we have roughly drawn it on the basis of morphology and petrography at the limit of detailed geologic mapping by Wolfe and others (1987). The relations of these rim basalts to the petrogenetic evolution of the SF field and to the deep-seated processes along the south margin of the Colorado Plateau remain topics for future analysis. Five major centers of intermediate to silicic rocks are located within the SF volcanic field (fig. 2). From west to east they are Bill Williams Mountain ( dacitic and andesitic domes and flows), Sitgreaves Mountain (rhyo­ litic domes), Kendrick Peak (andesitic to rhyolitic domes and flows), San Francisco Mountain (a stratovolcano dominantly made up of andesitic flows wi

(a stratovolcano dominantly made up of andesitic flows with dacitic and rhyolitic domes and flows) and O'Leary Peak ( andesitic to rhyolitic domes and flows). Several regional normal fault systems of late Cen­ ozoic age (fig. 2) cut the Paleozoic sedimentary rocks and locally affect rocks of the SF field as well. These fault systems have been shown by Shoemaker and others (1978) to be related to large, ancient systems of faults that cut the Proterozoic crystalline basement. A major one, the Mesa Butte fault system, trends northeast across the SF volcanic field. Several silicic to intermediate volcanic centers, including Bill Williams Mountain, Sit­ greaves Mountain, and Kendrick Peak, occur along or close to this fault system, which cuts some of the volcanic rocks (Ulrich and Nealey, 1976). The north-trending Oak Creek Canyon fault system cuts some cinder cones north of Oak Creek Canyon (Wolfe and others, 1987a). The north limit of this system is unknown because of burial; however, its projection places it beneath San Francisco Mountain. Minor faults of the Cataract Creek fault system trend northwest across the eastern part of the SF volcanic field. Tanaka, T.C. Onstott,1 and E.M. Shoemaker Abstract We present remanent magnetizations determined for 657 sites of volcanic rocks in the San Francisco volcanic field, an area of about 4,800 km2 in the southern part of the Colorado Plateau. The field includes scattered basaltic cinder cones and flows as well as silicic and intermediate rocks mostly in voluminous eruptive centers. About 90 percent of the sites yielded clear polarity determinations; the remainder have scattered data (a95 > 40°) or peculiar directions. Com­ prehensive stratigraphic controls-paleomagnetic polarity data, K-Ar and other absolute-age determinations, superpo­ sition relations, and lithologic associations-and state of preservation of the cinder cones provide a basis for age assignments of 503 separate eruptions related to basaltic vents and flows and 80 silicic to intermediate domes, flows, and flow sequences. Often these sites are diamagnetic. This indicates that their susceptibility is dominated by contributions from the carbonate matrix over contributions from ferromagnetic car- riers. Class A samples are inferred to be distinguished from class B and class C samples only by their abundance of magnetite. No other rock magnetic parameters, such as Koenigsberger ratio or median destructive temperature, appear associated with assigned class of remanence. Fold-test results The mean HSC directions of sites with class A and class B remanences are reported in Table 2. The directions are far better clustered after, rather than before, tectonic correction (Fig. 4). An unambiguously positive paleomagnetic fold test requires that maximum clustering occur on 100% untilting (Watson and Enkin 1993). ion of the structures in the Hosmer-Broadwood fold test occurred during a normal chron prior to the beginning of CLNS, but no older than Jurassic. The structures, themselves, are prob- ably post-Albian, or younger, but pre-Maastrichtian in age. Mechanism of remagnetization We propose that a similar mechanism is responsible for the magnetization at each locality, due to the similar character- istics of the magnetization and the consistent sequence of magnetic and tectonic events. Yet, we have not determined the mechanism responsible for the predeformational remag- netization. At all three localities, the stable magnetic carrier is magnetite with similar alternating-field and thermal- unblocking spectra. Thin sections exhibit diagenetic textures that require additional study to determine whether there is a relationship among optical textures, mineral paragenesis, and the HSC of the magnetism. Thus the paleomagnetic fold test provides a useful tool for the analysis of orogenic remagnetizations, whereas the drift of the continents through time relative to the magnetic pole provides a clock that potentially dates the remagnetizations and constrains the motions on individual structures. Sampling and analysis This study reports (Fig. 1; Table 1) on a traverse through the Foreland Belt in southwestern Alberta and southeastern British Columbia. Park Abstract: The rift-related Rapitan Group of the Mackenzie Mountains of northwestern Canada acquired several magnetizations due to pulses of hydrothermal activity. The first pulse, attributed to initiation of Rapitan rifting, produced a widespread overprint (P2) that may be reflected in the basal Mount Berg Formation. Two later pulses produced overprints similar to components found in an earlier study. Development of iron formation and hematite pigment in the overlying Sayunei Formation is attributed to the second pulse, represented by a paleopole (N = 10 sites; 334"E, 01 "S; 6p, 6m = 4", 9") that coincides with poles of the Franklin igneous events of northern Canada. The Franklin episode, suggested on geological grounds to be coeval with Sayunei deposition, dates the Sayunei at ca. 725 Ma. This relation implies that rifting in Mackenzie Mountains could be related to rifting in northern Canada. A third pulse, reflected by a pole at 007"E, 16"N (N = 6 sites; 6p, 6m = 6", 12"), is attributed to final rifting during deposition of the Shezal Formation at the top of the Rapitan. O

of the Yangzi (South China) Block. A palaeomagnetic study is reported here of the upper sequence (~ 730-670 Ma) which contains red beds. An 'AI' component (D/I= 291/-57 °, a95 = 5.0°, Palaeopole 151.2°E, 0.2°N) is resolved at high unblocking temperatures and resides in specular haematite. A study of contemporaneous deformation structures suggests that this component was acquired at an early stage of lithification and yields a representative palaeolatitude (37 °) for the glaciation. Lower blocking temperature magnetizations referred to as 'A2' (D/I=297/--19 °, ~t95 =7.6 °, Palaeopole 171.8°E, 19.2°S) and 'A3' (D/1=319/-1 °, ct95=3.2 °, Palaeopole 169.1°E, 41.8°S) are later overprints correlating with probable Late Precambrian or Cambrian palaeofields. In other regions, the 'A' magnetizations were found to be partially or completely overprinted by a Recent field and/or a 'B' remanence (D/I=4/13°); the latter correlates with a remagnetization widely recorded elsewhere in South China and is attributed to the Mesozoic Indosinian Orogeny. An ~ 90 ° apparent polar wander (APW) swathe is identified from the Yangzi Block between ~ 730-670 Ma and 540 Ma. It is not yet clear whether poles from older Sinian rocks record earlier magnetizations or were overprinted during this APW motion. Co

Studies of orogenic remagne- tization elsewhere have observed a relationship to advancing fluid fronts imparting secondary rema- nence at various stages of folding. Whilst rema- nence may be determined as pre-, syn- or post- deformational by reference to folded structures, it is ultimately part of the same event (Setiabudidaya et al., 1994). The best possibility for recovering a pre-orogenic remanence is afforded by the least- strained rocks. In the present example, these com- prise little-deformed platformal successions within the interior of the block. Because the conventional palaeomagnetic fold test is not then effective, pene- contemporaneous deformational structures have been used to assess the age of magnetization. Samples were collected as short cores with porta- ble drills and oriented by Sun and magnetic com- passes prior to extraction; these were subsequently cut into 2.3 cm length cylinders for palaeomagnetic processing. Magnetizations were measured by SQUID magnetometer and all cores were subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization using Magnetic Measurements (MM2D) demagnetizers. 3-199 1. Introduction The last few years have seen a heightened interest in the Neoproterozoic Earth. This has come, in part, from recognition of the important and enig- matic changes in the biosphere during these times (Knoll and Walter, 1992; Dalziel et al., 1994). This interest has also prompted a re-evaluation of Neoproterozoic glaciation because glacial rocks of this age are often a part of distinctive facies associations; the diamictites frequently occur interbedded with rocks more often assigned to low latitudes such as carbonates, red beds and phos- phorites (Schemerhorn, 1974; Hambrey and Harland, 1981; Harland, 1983; Fairchild et al., 1994). Whether or not lowland ice sheets actually occu- pied latitudes much lower than Permo- Carboniferous and Quaternary ice has, however, been the subject of much recent debate (e.g. Meert and Van der Voo, 1994; Williams et al., 1995; Young, 1995). This debate has a bearing on such questions as the obliquity of the Earth during Neoproterozoic times (e.g. Williams, 1993). A recent palaeomagnetic study of ~600Ma Marinoan periglacial rocks in South Australia has established unequivocally that they were formed close to the ancient equator as defined by the axial geocentric dipole model (Schmidt and Williams, 1995).

3-199 1. Introduction The last few years have seen a heightened interest in the Neoproterozoic Earth. This has come, in part, from recognition of the important and enig- matic changes in the biosphere during these times (Knoll and Walter, 1992; Dalziel et al., 1994). This interest has also prompted a re-evaluation of Neoproterozoic glaciation because glacial rocks of this age are often a part of distinctive facies associations; the diamictites frequently occur interbedded with rocks more often assigned to low latitudes such as carbonates, red beds and phos- phorites (Schemerhorn, 1974; Hambrey and Harland, 1981; Harland, 1983; Fairchild et al., 1994). Whether or not lowland ice sheets actually occu- pied latitudes much lower than Permo- Carboniferous and Quaternary ice has, however, been the subject of much recent debate (e.g. Meert and Van der Voo, 1994; Williams et al., 1995; Young, 1995). This debate has a bearing on such questions as the obliquity of the Earth during Neoproterozoic times (e.g. Williams, 1993). A recent palaeomagnetic study of ~600Ma Marinoan periglacial rocks in South Australia has established unequivocally that they were formed close to the ancient equator as defined by the axial geocentric dipole model (Schmidt and Williams, 1995).

carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: , A.P. 89000, Caracas 1060-A, Venezuela Received 7 May 1996; accepted 11 March 1997 Abstract We report paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data from the rapakivi granites of the Parguaza batholith (Guyana Precambrian Shield, southwestern Venezuela). These results suggest that the pluton is inversely zoned with respect to the cooling ages. In order to explain such an age pattern, tentative structural settings are proposed placing the Parguaza intrusions in a plate tectonic context. Six sites were sampled along a 200 km transect that cuts through the northern lobe of the batholith. Therrnomagnetic curves, X-ray diffraction and fluorescence, hysteresis loops, thermal and alternating field (AF) intensity plots, transmission (TEM) and scanning (SEM) electron microscope analyses and Krnigsberger ratios (Q, values) were used to identify the different magnetic mineralogies and their distribution of grain sizes. Magnetite, titanomagnetite near magnetite in composition and deuteric hematite are the three carriers of natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) in these rocks. Magnetic granulometry indicators such as Krnigsberger ratios (Qn values) suggest the dominant presence of single domain magnetites with average grain sizes grading from finer to coarser away from the center of the transect.

Thus, according to this model, the Parguaza granites would be considered as anorogenic intrusions in a subducted plate. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: , A.P. 89000, Caracas 1060-A, Venezuela Received 7 May 1996; accepted 11 March 1997 Abstract We report paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data from the rapakivi granites of the Parguaza batholith (Guyana Precambrian Shield, southwestern Venezuela). These results suggest that the pluton is inversely zoned with respect to the cooling ages. In order to explain such an age pattern, tentative structural settings are proposed placing the Parguaza intrusions in a plate tectonic context. Six sites were sampled along a 200 km transect that cuts through the northern lobe of the batholith. Therrnomagnetic curves, X-ray diffraction and fluorescence, hysteresis loops, thermal and alternating field (AF) intensity plots, transmission (TEM) and scanning (SEM) electron microscope analyses and Krnigsberger ratios (Q, values) were used to identify the different magnetic mineralogies and their distribution of grain sizes. Magnetite, titanomagnetite near magnetite in composition and deuteric hematite are the three carriers of natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) in these rocks. Magnetic granulometry indicators such as Krnigsberger ratios (Qn values) suggest the dominant presence of single domain magnetites with average grain sizes grading from finer to coarser away from the center of the transect.

These results suggest that the pluton is inversely zoned with respect to the cooling ages. In order to explain such an age pattern, tentative

ps, thermal and alternating field (AF) intensity plots, transmission (TEM) and scanning (SEM) electron microscope analyses and Krnigsberger ratios (Q, values) were used to identify the different magnetic mineralogies and their distribution of grain sizes. Magnetite, titanomagnetite near magnetite in composition and deuteric hematite are the three carriers of natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) in these rocks. Magnetic granulometry indicators such as Krnigsberger ratios (Qn values) suggest the dominant presence of single domain magnetites with average grain sizes grading from finer to coarser away from the center of the transect. The paleomagnetic results reveal the existence of two primary thermoremanent and/or thermochemical magnetizations (TRMs/TCRMs) for sites CSP-3, PI-2 and PI-4 (Decl. = 328 °, Incl.= -21 °, k=15, a95=11.4 °) and sites CSP-2, PI-I and PI-3 (Decl.= 16 °, Incl.=87 °, k= 10, ~95= 13°), respectively. By the same token, namely by looking at the spatial distribution of time- calibrated paleomagnetic data, it should also be possible to establish the pattern of cooling for a batholith of considerable proportions. A con- tinuous variation of distinctive vector directions for different components of remanence would be expected on a transect that cuts through the intru- sion's internal zoning. Lower Paleocene Tarkhov Formation NRM intensity of the Tarkhov tuffaceous rocks vary widely (Table 2), both at the within-locality and between-locality levels. For instance, weakly mag- netized varieties were found in interlayers up to 3 m thick at localities T1 and T2, whereas such varieties prevail at locality T3, with the only 30-cm-thick layer of high magnetic rocks at the site base. The San Luis Basin is the largest of four tilted, fault bounded Neogene basins of the northern Rio Grande rift in New Mexico and Colorado. It formed during the second of two episodes of extension beginning in middle Oligocene and extending to the present. The San Luis Hills are an intrarift horst of Oligocene intermediate and basalt rocks preserved in the middle of the San Luis Basin. Previous paleomagnetic and structural studies in the Espanola Basin to the south indicate counterclockwise rotation of that region during the most re- cent extension. Introduction The Rio Grande rift is an intracontinental rift that extends from northern Mexico to central Colorado. The central and northern part of the rift is composed of the north-trending Albuquerque, Espanola, San Luis and upper Arkansas basins, which are filled with Neogene (mostly Miocene) sedimentary and volcanic rocks. The largest of these basins, the San Luis basin, is covered in the southern part by the Taos Plateau vol- canic field, a Pliocene dominantly basaltic volcanic field (Lipman and Mehnert, 1979). An intrarift horst of Oligocene igneous rocks, the San Luis Hills, is present just north of the Taos Plateau in southernmost Colorado (Figure 1). The rift appears to have undergone two distinct phases of extension beginning in the middle Oligocene (Morgan and Golombek, 1984; Morgan et al., 1986). The early phase of extension was temporally and spatially associated with major magmatic events and locally involved very large strains, typi- cally on closely spaced low-angle or listric normal faults. We try here to answer this important question with the paleomagnetic study of well dated Permo-Triassic sediments from a borehole in Saudi Arabia. Sediments of the same age have also been sampled at the surface, but proved to be remagnetized, probably by a strong desert alteration. The paleomagnetic study of the bore-hole core yielded a high temperature component magnetization thought to be of primary origin carried either by magnetite (Late Permian limestones) or hematite (Early Triassic red shales) with antipodal normal and reversed inclinations. Sequence stratigraphy, based on two-dimensional analysis of outcrops, formed the stratigraphic framework for the magnetostratigraphic study. Rock magnetic analyses showed that magnetite is the dominant ferromagnetic mineral in the limestones. Both alternating field and thermal demagnetization were satisfactory in defining two main components in the weak magnetizations. A component with low coercivity. low unblocking temperature and normal polarity was close in direction to the present axial dipole field direction at the site. A higher coercivity, higher unblocking temperature component with both polarities was interpreted as the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM). Although the mean directions of samples with normal and reversed polarity are not exactly antipodal. a stratigraphic sequence of magnetozones is very clearly defined. The Pennapiedimonte magnetostratigraphy correlates well with late Cretaceous Chrons C30r to C34n in the established polarity timescale; numerical ages can thus be allocated to the reversals. From the latest Cretaceous to Oligocene, phases of subaerial and submarine erosion alternated with phases of prevailing platform aggradation and progradation along this platform margin [17]. A sec- ond progradation took place during the late Eocene (Priabonian) to Oligocene (Supersequence 5). It was preceded by a late Paleocene to middle Eocene interval of slope deposition and erosion (Superse- quences 3 and 4). In the late Oligocene and early Miocene the Maiella platform was deeply eroded. From the latest Cretaceous to Oligocene, phases of subaerial and submarine erosion alternated with phases of prevailing platform aggradation and progradation along this platform margin [17]. A sec- ond progradation took place during the late Eocene (Priabonian) to Oligocene (Supersequence 5). It was preceded by a late Paleocene to middle Eocene interval of slope deposition and erosion (Superse- quences 3 and 4). In the late Oligocene and early Miocene the Maiella platform was deeply eroded. During the latest Oligocene to early Miocene a tem- perate carbonate shelf was established in the area (Supersequence 6). Extensive erosion under subaerial conditions took place during the Messinian, ending the evolution of carbonate platforms in central Italy. During the Miocene-Pliocene the carbonate platforms of the external Apennines were involved in thrusting and folding, resulting in stacked thrust sheets that strike mainly northwest-southeast and verge northeast [ 141. The reported successful magnetostrati- graphic correlations between the Lower Triassic Werfen Formation from the Dolomites [24] and the composite polarity sequence of the Canadian Arctic [25] suggest that the Dolomites (and hence Hydra) were most probably in the northern hemisphere in the Middle Triassic, in agreement with the most recent paleogeographic reconstructions of Pangea (e.g., [26]). A northern hemisphere location since the Middle Triassic would also imply that the post-fold- ing “B” component overprint in the Aghia Triada and Vlichos sections was acquired during a period of reversed polarity. The north paleomagnetic pole corresponding to the characteristic component from Friitschbach (Ta- ble 1) falls near Middle Triassic paleopoles from other regions in the Southern Alps which have West Gondwana affinity [26]. Indeed, data from the South- em Alps, and particularly the Friitschbach pole, were used [26] to refine the APWP of West Gondwana [27]. The Frijtschbach/Seceda section includes two radiometrically dated (U-Pb) tuff levels and covers two of the three chief candidates for the position of the base of the Ladinian, namely at the base of the Secedensis Zone or the subsequent Curionii Zone. The Aghia Triada section yields biochronological evidence for the base of the Secedensis Zone, whose significance is, however, critically discussed in the light of the magnetostratigraphic correlation with Friitschbach/Seceda. The Vlichos section can be correlated with Aghia Triada and Friitschbach/Seceda by means of magnetic polarity stratigraphy and sparse fossil occurrences. The satisfactory correlation of the magnetozones allows us to construct a composite geomagnetic polarity sequence tied to Tethyan ammonoid and conodont biostratigraphy for about a 2.4 Myr interval across the Anisian/Ladinian boundary. The Frijtschbach/Seceda section includes two radiometrically dated (U-Pb) tuff levels and covers two of the three chief candidates for the position of the base of the Ladinian, namely at the base of the Secedensis Zone or the subsequent Curionii Zone. The Aghia Triada section yields biochronological evidence for the base of the Secedensis Zone, whose significance is, however, critically discussed in the light of the magnetostratigraphic correlation with Friitschbach/Seceda. section_candidates.excerpt: (U-Pb) tuff levels and covers two of the three chief candidates for the position of the base of the Ladinian, namely at the base of the Secedensis Zone or the subsequent Curionii Zone. The Aghia Triada section yields biochronological evidence for the base of the Secedensis Zone, whose significance is, however, critically discussed in the light of the magnetostratigraphic correlation with Friitschbach/Seceda. The Vlichos section can be correlated with Aghia Triada and Friitschbach/Seceda by means of magnetic polarity stratigraphy and sparse fossil occurrences. The satisfactory correlation of the magnetozones allows us to construct a composite geomagnetic polarity sequence tied to Tethyan ammonoid and conodont biostratigraphy for about a 2.4 Myr interval across the Anisian/Ladinian boundary. We argue that these ages are erroneous for the following reasons: (1) The >2 Ma spread in the ages is inconsistent with the paleomagnetic data (of very high precision, k = 126) and the petrological evidence, which indicate that the Selkirk Volcanics were erupted over hundreds of years or less, not millions of years. Else- where, the presence of these in young, low-K basalts has been associated with significant excess mantle-derived Ar, causing anomalously old age determinations (Dalrymple and Moore 1968). Irving Abstract: The paleomagnetism of the Selkirk Volcanics and nearby stratified Pleistocene sediments was investigated to resolve the chronology of Early Pleistocene glaciations in central Yukon. Radiometric dates on these low-K basalts have proven to be erroneously old. Most sampled sediments and all basalts accurately record the paleofield and true reversals. The valley-filling phase of the Selkirk Volcanics was in part coeval with the younger pre-Reid glaciation. It was erupted during the Matuyarna Chron, either post-Cobb Mountain Subchron or post-Jararnillo Subchron, over a period too brief to average secular variation. The older pre-Reid glaciation occurred after ca. 1.60 Ma and prior to the eruption of the Fort Selkirk tephra (pre-Jaramillo or pre-Cobb Mountain). Sediments investigated at Revenue Creek and Braden's Canyon are normally magnetized. The assigned B

id glaciation occurred after ca. 1.60 Ma and prior to the eruption of the Fort Selkirk tephra (pre-Jaramillo or pre-Cobb Mountain). Sediments investigated at Revenue Creek and Braden's Canyon are normally magnetized. It is well known that in basalts magnetite is a product of high-temperature heterophase oxidation of primary magmatic titanomagnetite. Such magnetite often has primary thermo- remanent magnetization (TRM). Tuffs are the result of the redeposition of the products of basaltic volcanism; that is why they contain mainly clastic magnetite, with which primary detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) should be associated. This notion is supported by the ratio of the NRM and the anhysteretic remanence (ARM). Basalt Sh127 (A magnetiz- ation) has NRM/ARM = 1.1, which does not contradict with the TRM nature of the NRM; basalt Sh151 (B magnetization) has NRM/ARM =0.1, which may be explained by a large viscous component in the NRM. Four tuffs with magnetization A have NRM/ARM in the range 0.09-0.3; such values are typical for the DRM. Palaeomagnetic and petromagnetic investigations of the Upper Cretaceous-Lower Palaeocene volcanics of the Kumroch Ridge at 12 localities (183 hand samples) were carried out to determine the movements of the subduction zone during volcanic activity. The major magnetic mineral in all rocks is low-Ti titanomagnetite, which is typical for island-arc basalt. Most of the titanomagnetite grains from basalts are homogenous, and their Curie points are 45O0-5O0"C; a small fraction of the magnetic grains have T, = 560"- 580°C. Most of the titanomagnetite grains in tuffs have been oxidized to magnetite. NRM stepwise thermal demagnetization was carried out, together with principal component analysis. As a result of fold, baked contact, conglomerate and 'long particles' tests, the high temperature, close to the primary, ChRM component was found. Mean palaeomagnetic directions for four stratigraphic intervals from the base to the top of the sequence are: (1) D=32", I=49", ccgs=3.8"; (2) D=218", Z=-56", cc,,=5.6"; (3) D = 251 O, I = - 66 O, ccgs = 2.7 "; (4) D = 230 ", I = - 69 ", ccg5 = 7.8 ". The mean palaeolati- tude changed from 30 " to 53 O during formation of the volcanic sequence. The drifting rate was 15-20 cm yr-', which is close to the independent estimation of the Kula plate rate for the same time. According to palaeodeclinations, the area investigated was rotated clockwise 30 "-70 O and rocks were partly remagnetized. Key words: palaeolat

Layered reworked basalt, andesite and more rare picrite tuffs dominate in their composition. Usually, an alternation of rocks containing fragments of different sizes, from agglomerates and breccia to sandy and muddy tuffs, is observed. Tuffites, in which pyroclasts are mixed with clayey and flinty material, are widely developed. Volcanic members and lenses are common in the sections where coarse-grained tuffs dominate. Konstantinovskaya et al. (1993) consider this complex as a volcanic flinty-tufaceous formation that was accumulated on the slopes of an ensimatic island arc. Low-K island-arc tholei- ites prevail in the basalts of the complex, while the fraction of calc-alkaline rocks is relatively small (Magakian et al. 1993); picrites are assumed to belong to the boninite series (Kamenetsky et al. 1993). Taken together, this allows us to compare these units with the volcanics of primitive oceanic island arcs (Zinkevich & Tsukanov 1993). These volcanic-sedimentary layers were highly deformed, resulting in a series of steep imbricated thrusts of southeast vergence. Occasionally, small gentle overthrust sheets were formed. itive oceanic island arcs (Zinkevich & Tsukanov 1993). These volcanic-sedimentary layers were highly deformed, resulting in a series of steep imbricated thrusts of southeast vergence. Occasionally, small gentle overthrust sheets were formed. The complicated tectonic structure together with sharp facies variations and rare palaeontological occurrences pre- vents us from making a detailed stratigraphic subdivision of the complex. The bottom of the complex does not crop out anywhere, and its upper part transforms concordantly to terrigenous flysch layers of the Talnikovsky (Valaginsky Ridge) and Drozdovsky (Tumrok and Kumroch ridges) Formations. A large fraction of radiolarians from the flinty rocks of the Valaginsky and Khapitsky Formations were determined to be of Upper Campanian to Maastrichtian age (Tsukanov 1991). The Upper Palaeocene plankton foraminifera were found in the lower part of the Talnikovsky flysch in the Valaginsky Ridge (Bakhteev et al. 1994). Thus, the upper part of the Valaginsky series could be of Lower Palaeocene age. Similar structures in Upper Campanian, Maastrichtian and Lower Palaeocene volcanic sedimentary complexes also devel- oped on the eastern slopes of the Sredinny Ridge (the Kirganiksky Formation) (Flyorov & Koloskov 1976) and in the s

The Upper Palaeocene plankton foraminifera were found in the lower part of the Talnikovsky flysch in the Valaginsky Ridge (Bakhteev et al. 1994). Thus, the upper part of the Valaginsky series could be of Lower Palaeocene age. Similar structures in Upper Campanian, Maastrichtian and Lower Palaeocene volcanic sedimentary complexes also devel- oped on the eastern slopes of the Sredinny Ridge (the Kirganiksky Formation) (Flyorov & Koloskov 1976) and in the southern part of the Koryak highland (the Achaivayam Formation) (Alekseev 1979). Many researchers consider these complexes, together with the complexes of the Eastern Ridge, as a single palaeoisland-arc system, which we name the Achaivayam-Valaginsky palaeoarc (Shapiro 1995). It is assumed that it was formed as an intra-oceanic arc, and later, due to northwestward drift, became part of Eurasia. The Upper Cretaceous and Lower Palaeocene volcanic island-arc complexes of Eastern Kamchatka, which formed on the Pacific ocean during rapid northward drift, satisfy the above conditions. Palaeomagnetic and petromagnetic investigations of the Upper Cretaceous-Lower Palaeocene volcanics of the Kumroch Ridge at 12 localities (183 hand samples) were carried out to determine the movements of the subduction zone during volcanic activity. The major magnetic mineral in all rocks is low-Ti titanomagnetite, which is typical for island-arc basalt. Most of the titanomagnetite grains from basalts are homogenous, and their Curie points are 45O0-5O0"C; a small fraction of the magnetic grains have T, = 560"- 580°C. Most of the titanomagnetite grains in tuffs have been oxidized to magnetite. NRM stepwise thermal demagnetization was carried out, together with principal component analysis. As a result of fold, baked contact, conglomerate and 'long particles' tests, the high temperature, close to the primary, ChRM component was found. It differs from the rocks of the lowest member by the overturned bedding (Table l), structural and textural charac- teristics and the degree of tuff zeolitization; usually it is considered as the lowermost part of the Khapitsky Formation. Cherty tuffites interlayered with tufaceous siltstone and sandy tuffs were sampled. 4 METHOD Hand samples from the outcrops were sampled manually and were orientated by magnetic compass. Each hand sample was cut into 1-3 cubic specimens with 2 cm ribs. Specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization in a furnace with a four-layer permalloy shield. After each heating, the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured on a JR-4 spin-magnetometer within large Helmholtz coils, and the magnetic susceptibility (k) was measured on a KLY-2 kappa- meter. k was measured not only for petromagnetic information but to control changes in the samples during laboratory heating. The results of the palaeomagnetic measurements were pro- cessed by NRM component analysis, great-circle analysis (Halls 1978), Graham conglomerate and fold tests, the reversal test, and the long-particle test (Pechersky 1970). INTRODUCTION For the late Quaternary, studies of palaeosecular variation from lake sediments, lavas and archaeological material are fairly plentiful from Europe, the USA and Japan, but very limited for the rest of the world, especially the regions with latitudes less than 30" in the Northern Hemisphere (e.g. Mexico) and the Southern Hemisphere. A better geographical coverage is required to refine models of geomagnetic field behaviour. The calculated values of the virtual dipole moment (VDM) range from 3.1 to 14.9 x A m2. During historical times, on the basis of direct observations of the geomagnetic field, it has been observed that the direction as well as the magnitude of the non-dipolar field, which produces the majority of the observed secular variation, has a very irregular distribution over the Earth's surface. This non- dipolar component is at the present time larger in the Southern Hemisphere than the Northern Hemisphere, and is almost non-existent in the Central Pacific region (Doell & Cox 1972). Analyses of late Quaternary palaeomagnetic results from Hawaii have tended to show a lower than predicted angular dispersion of virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs), both from lavas (Doell & Cox 1972; McWilliams, Holcomb & Champion 1982) and from sedimentary sequences (Peng & King 1992). At the same time another group from UNAM were trying to obtain a record of palaeosecular variation from late Quaternary lacustrine sediments from Lake Chalco, close to Mexico City (Ortega-Guerrero 1992; Urrutia Fucugauchi et al. 1995). We present the results of a detailed study of geomagnetic secular variation recorded by lavas from two separate volcanic fields in the Transmexican Volcanic Belt, located in Central Mexico (Fig. 1): (a) the Michoacan-Guanajuato volcanic field (MGVF) located north of Uruapan; (b) the Chichinautzin Formation, south of Mexico City. These volcanic fields consist principally of monogenetic cinder cones that have, in the majority of cases, lavas interstrati- fied with the ashes or volcanic scoria. A characteristic of these monogenetic volcanoes is that they are active only for a short period and then become extinct; in the case of Paricutin in the MGVF, activity started in February 1943 and continued for nine years. AII the sampling was carried out in lavas from these monogenetic volcanoes. THE KERGUELEN ISLANDS Numerous arguments have been advanced to show that the Kerguelen archipelago (Fig. 1) is oceanic, rather than a conti- nental fragment. No rocks older than 39 Ma have been found in these islands (Giret & Lameyre 1982). Granites, which crop out mainly in the southwestern part of the Kerguelen Islands, resulted from the differentiation of mantle magma (Bonin & Lameyre 1978; Dosso et al. 1976). The basement of the Kerguelen Plateau is basaltic (Leclaire et al. 1987). The crust under the Kerguelen Islands is 13-17 km thick (Recq, Charvis & Hirn 1983; Recq & Charvis 1986; Recq et al. 1990), with an underplating of magma of mantle origin (GrCgoire et al. 1992). Very small grains of Ti-poor titanomagnetites (or titanomaghemites) probably correspond to a relatively early phase, and larger grains of Ti-rich titanomagnetite to a late magmatic phase. PALAEOMAGNETIC ANALYSIS To limit the contribution of the viscous magnetization observed in several flows, the samples were kept in a zero field for at least six months. The Zijderveld diagrams show two different demagnetization behaviours depending on the site (Fig. 7). In the Port Douzieme, Port Jeanne #Arc and Puy Saint Theodule sections, a single component appears in the majority of the flows. In the Port Couvreux and Val Studer sites, two compo- nents are usually observed. The problem is to determine, for the samples with a single component, if this component corresponds to the low-coercivity or high-coercivity compo- nent of the samples with two components. Fortunately, some samples from Port Douzikme, Port Jeanne &Arc and Puy Saint Theodule sections have two components, and it is clear that the single component in these sites is equivalent to the high-coercivity one. Figs 8 and 9 show, respectively, the orientations of the low- and high-coercivity components. The Zijderveld diagrams also show the existence of a very high-coercivity component by the fact that the regression lines associated with the high-blocking-field component do not cross the origin of the axes exactly for numerous samples (Fig. 7). The virtual dipole moment at ca. 2.8 Ga is 1.9 & 0.6 x 10" Am2, which is about one- quarter of the present value. Key words: Archaean, Earth's core, geomagnetic field, Greenland, K-Ar age, palaeomagnetism. INTRODUCTION The magnetic field behaviour of the early Earth provides significant information about the evolution of the Earth's core. The timing of separation from a primitive core to the present stratified core might be estimated through the appearance of a fairly strong geomagnetic field on a billion-year timescale in terms of the energetics of the core (Stevenson, Spohn & Shubert 1983). Palaeo-geomagnetic intensity data compiled by Hale (1987a) from Archaean rocks of the African and Canadian shields with ages between 3.5 Ga and 0.8 Ga suggest that a marked increase in magnitude of the geomagnetic field occurred between 2.7 Ga and 2.1 Ga. A recent compilation of the most reliable palaeointensity data by Prevot & Perrin

ata compiled by Hale (1987a) from Archaean rocks of the African and Canadian shields with ages between 3.5 Ga and 0.8 Ga suggest that a marked increase in magnitude of the geomagnetic field occurred between 2.7 Ga and 2.1 Ga. A recent compilation of the most reliable palaeointensity data by Prevot & Perrin (1992), however, hardly recognizes this palaeointensity increase. This is because of a shortage of data within this interval. The accumulation of more palaeointensity data from Archean times is therefore required to show the evolution of the core. The present study aims to investigate the palaeointensity for an Archaean dolerite dyke in west Greenland (Fig. 1). The Archaean gneiss complex, with radiometric ages between * Present address: Faculty of Education, Kochi University, Kochi 780, Japan. 3800 Ma and 2900 Ma, is exposed in the southwestern part of Greenland (Escher & Watt 1976; Nutman et al. 1989; McGregor, Friend & Nutman 1991). Major dolerite swarms were emplaced into the Archaean gneiss after the end of plutonic activity at about 2700-2500 Ma (Nielsen 1985). European plate motions during Triassic-Lower Jurassic times, new palaeomagnetic data were acquired from various Triassic-Liassic sediments of northeastern France and southwestern Germany. A Carnian palaeopole 49"N/13 1 "E, K = 193, A,, = 7", N =4 was obtained for Keuper marls with consistent directions of normal and reversed polarities. Rhaetian sandstones, also with both polarities, and Carnian dolomites with a magnetization of probable secondary origin, provide a mean pole 51°N/112"E, K= 109, Ag5=6", N=6, more westerly than that given above. The Lower Hettangian, sampled in limestones of the Xeuilley quarry near Nancy shows a N-R-N polarity sequence with well-defined anti-parallel directions. The mean Hettangian pole is 55"N/10OoE, K = 123, Ag5 = 1 lo, N = 3. Induan sandstones from the northern Vosges show two distinct overprints, one consistent with the Ladinian- Carnian magnetizations already observed in the same region, the second consistent with the recalculated mean Lower Jurassic pole of Europe. Five other sites with different rock types also exhibit late overprints with Lower Jurassic directions. The mean pole calculated from these overprints is 74"N/124"E, K = 125, A,, = 6", N = 6. The revised apparent polar wander path (APWP) presented here shows that for the mid-Permian to the earliest Jurassic the palaeopoles of Europe stayed around 50" latitude, while the longitudes drifted from 185"E to 100"E. After the late Alleghanian tectonic phase, which marked the end of the Variscan orogeny, central western Europe rotated counterclockwise during about 70 Myr, up to the earliest Jurassic. magnetic measurements together with comparison with weight percent iron demonstrate that anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility is carried by paramagnetic biotite and tourmaline. The latter produces an inverse fabric, i.e. with the minimum axis parallel to mineral lineation. The magnetic fabric demonstrates complex patterns of stretching lineations during magmatic emplacement, and its usefulness in semi-quantitatively estimating petrofabric intensity is demonstrated for the biotite-bearing facies. Natural remanent magnetization was measurable at only two sites in Everest-Makalu, where there are well-defined reverse directions carried by titanomagnetite and pyrrhotite. Comparison of these preliminary results with predicted directions for stable India suggests northward tilting of about 10 ° and a small clockwise rotation of this massif. 1. This NW-SE-elongated Carboniferous-Permian basin of about 600 km 2 is unconformably covered by Triassic-Jurassic formations. The northeastern bor- der is often a normal fault; however, the primary con- tact is a stratigraphic one, since Carboniferous and Permian rocks unconformably overlie the Limousin metamorphic rocks with basal conglomerate and coarse sandstone. The southern border corresponds to a series of NW-SE-trending faults, namely from west to east: the Ch~tre, Condat and Meyssac faults. This method facilitated a more ac- curate identification of magnetic carriers (Fig. 2). For the Portlandian (sites 37 and 48; Fig. 2a,b), Aptian (sites 38 and 46, Fig. 2d,e) and Albian (site 40, Fig. 2f) the experiment demonstrates the pres- ence of two magnetic carriers: one that is not satu- rated by fields of 1.2 T and whose unblocking temperature occurs at 12O”C, and another that has weak coercivities and unblocking temperatures up to 500°C. Our study yields a paleopole for the Portlandian-Valanginian (4 = 256”, A = 58”, A,, = 5”) and a paleopole for the Aptian-Albian (4 = 232”, A = 75”, A,, = 8”). These results allow better constraint of the relative rotation of Iberia with respect to Europe: this rotation of 22” + 14” is a rather fast event occurring during the Barremian, between 132 and 124 Ma. The sections span the interval from 15 _ 2 to 135 +_ 4 ka, with large hiatuses. Rock magnetic investigations indicate that the natural remanent magnetisation (NRM) is carried by titanomagnetites in the four oldest sections, with a contribution from high coercivity magnetic minerals in the youngest section. Palaeomagnetic directions obtained by thermal demagnetisation document a large magnetic excursion, at around 110 ka, with virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) that lie over eastern Siberia. These directions may represent a volcanic record of the termination of the Blake event. Only about 15% of the samples (from 19 flows) proved suitable for palaeointensity (Thellier and TheUier) determinations. Palaeomagnetic directions obtained by thermal demagnetisation document a large magnetic excursion, at around 110 ka, with virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) that lie over eastern Siberia. These directions may represent a volcanic record of the termination of the Blake event. Only about 15% of the samples (from 19 flows) proved suitable for palaeointensity (Thellier and TheUier) determinations. Etna for the period from 140 to 60 ka (Tricet al., 1994, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 85:113-129), these results document a broad low at around 115 ka. The palaeointensity values from Vulcano and Etna are consistent with global values, suggesting the presence of a dominant dipole-field contribution. Three-hundred and twelve paleomagnetic samples were collected from 73 sites within a 350-m continuously exposed ¯at-lying section. The section is characterized by alternating packages of well-developed paleosol mudstone horizons (Wasatch Formation) and lacustrine shale/lime- stone horizons (Green River Formation). Fossil mammal assemblages are known from various levels within the section and constrain the location of the Wasatchian/Bridgerian NALMA boundary to lie between 60 and 120 m. Paleomag- netic results of paleosol horizons are generally characterized by two components, a present-day ®eld component with low unblocking temperatures up to 400°C, and a characteristic component with unblocking temperatures up to 680°C. Characteristic magnetizations have either N-NW and steeply down directions or antipodal S-SE and up directions. The characteristic component is interpreted as primary based on antipodal polarity directions and congruence with the expected Eocene direction for western Wyoming. Results indicate that the ®rst 30 m of section are characterized by normal polarity, the next 230 m by dominantly reversed polarity, followed by a 70 m interval of alternating polarity. We conclude that the A- and C-components are normal over- prints, primarily due to partial remagnetization in a recent field, and contaminated by an unre- moved element of the B-component. The A-com- ponent is probably a simple viscous overprint. The C-component is defined in a range of un- blocking temperatures above the Curie point of maghemite. It was not possible to identify the magnetic mineral carrying this component defini- tively. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: elded tufts have been sampled for chronological and palaeomagnetic studies from the northern part of central Japan. Zircon fission-track dating confirms Middle to Late Miocene ages (13.7-5.0 Ma) for the Yatakezawa, Shiobara, Kawaji, Kinugawa, Katashinagawa, Okkai and Ashio Formations. Characteristic directions with high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 36 sites. Palaeomagnetic directions after tilt correction provide a Miocene characteristic palaeomagnetic direction of the northern part of central Japan (36.8°N, 139.3°E): D = 7.3 °, 1 = 50.3 °, a95 = 6.6 °. Presence of normal and reversed polarities, and a fairly long time average exclude the effect of geomagnetic field secular variation. Comparison with the Miocene palaeomagnetic poles of the neighbouring blocks indicates that the northern part of central Japan and northeast Japan behaved as a unified block since 15 Ma, whereas the Kanto Mountain region moved kinematically as an independent block from the northern block comprised of central Japan and northeast Japan at least between 16 Ma and 12 Ma. esence of normal and reversed polarities, and a fairly long time average exclude the effect of geomagnetic field secular variation. Comparison with the Miocene palaeomagnetic poles of the neighbouring blocks indicates that the northern part of central Japan and northeast Japan behaved as a unified block since 15 Ma, whereas the Kanto Mountain region moved kinematically as an independent block from the northern block comprised of central Japan and northeast Japan at least between 16 Ma and 12 Ma. The boundary between the northern part of central Japan and the Kanto Mountain was in a convergent regime with dextral strike slip. A southward force exerted from the northern part of central Japan, as well as a northward force by the Izu-Bonin ridge, induced the clockwise rotation of the Kanto Mountain region. section_candidates.excerpt: ES 537-550, JUNE 1997 Palcomagnetic evidence for rapid vertical-axis rotations during thrusting in an active collision zone, northeastern Papua New Guinea Peter D. Weiler and Robert S. Coe Department of Earth Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of three thrust sheets of the fold and thrust belt north of the Ramu-Markham Fault Zone (RMFZ) indicates very rapid vertical-axis rotations, with differential declination anomalies related to tectonic transport of thrust units. Data from this investigation indicate depositional ages straddling the Brun_hes-Matuyama reversal (780 ka) for the Leron Formation in Erap Valley. Net counterclockwise, vertical-axis rotations as great as 90 ø since 1 Ma have occurred locally in the Erap Valley area. These rotations appear to be kinematically related to shear across a tear fault within the foreland fold and thrust belt of the colliding Finisterre Are, which in turn is aligned with and may be slructurally controlled by a major fault in the lower plate. These data indicate that vertical-axis rotations occurred during thrusting; consequently, the actual rotation rate is likely several times higher than the calculated minimum rate. Such very rapid rotations during thrust sheet eraplacement may be

ed lineations that differ markedly in azimuth in the three thrust sheets. The susceptibility lineations are rendered parallel by the same bedding-perpendicular rotations used to restore the palcomagnetic remanence to N-S thus independently confirming the rapid rotations. The restored lineations are perpendicular to the direction of tectonic transport, and the minimum susceptibility axes are slxeaked perpendicular to the lineation. We interpret these anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility data as primary sedimentary fabrics modified by weak strain accompanying foreland thrusting. section_candidates.excerpt: ES 537-550, JUNE 1997 Palcomagnetic evidence for rapid vertical-axis rotations during thrusting in an active collision zone, northeastern Papua New Guinea Peter D. Weiler and Robert S. Coe Department of Earth Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of three thrust sheets of the fold and thrust belt north of the Ramu-Markham Fault Zone (RMFZ) indicates very rapid vertical-axis rotations, with differential declination anomalies related to tectonic transport of thrust units. Data from this investigation indicate depositional ages straddling the Brun_hes-Matuyama reversal (780 ka) for the Leron Formation in Erap Valley. Net counterclockwise, vertical-axis rotations as great as 90 ø since 1 Ma have occurred locally in the Erap Valley area. These rotations appear to be kinematically related to shear across a tear fault within the foreland fold and thrust belt of the colliding Finisterre Are, which in turn is aligned with and may be slructurally controlled by a major fault in the lower plate. These data indicate that vertical-axis rotations occurred during thrusting; consequently, the actual rotation rate is likely several times higher than the calculated minimum rate. Such very rapid rotations during thrust sheet eraplacement may be

ed lineations that differ markedly in azimuth in the three thrust sheets. The susceptibility lineations are rendered parallel by the same bedding-perpendicular rotations used to restore the palcomagnetic remanence to N-S thus independently confirming the rapid rotations. The restored lineations are perpendicular to the direction of tectonic transport, and the minimum susceptibility axes are slxeaked perpendicular to the lineation. We interpret these anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility data as primary sedimentary fabrics modified by weak strain accompanying foreland thrusting. Geologists now recognize vertical-axis block rotations, resolved through palcomagnetic declination anomalies, as a common consequence of crustal deformation, particularly in settings with strike-slip motion but also in settings characterized by thrusting [e.g., Beck, 1976; Simpson and Cox, 1977; Schwartz and Van der Voo, 1984; Luyendyk et al., 1985: Coe et al., 1985; Wells and Heller, 1988; Fuller, et al., 1989]. section_candidates.excerpt: ES 537-550, JUNE 1997 Palcomagnetic evidence for rapid vertical-axis rotations during thrusting in an active collision zone, northeastern Papua New Guinea Peter D. Weiler and Robert S. Coe Department of Earth Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of three thrust sheets of the fold and thrust belt north of the Ramu-Markham Fault Zone (RMFZ) indicates very rapid vertical-axis rotations, with differential declination anomalies related to tectonic transport of thrust units. Data from this investigation indicate depositional ages straddling the Brun_hes-Matuyama reversal (780 ka) for the Leron Formation in Erap Valley. Net counterclockwise, vertical-axis rotations as great as 90 ø since 1 Ma have occurred locally in the Erap Valley area. These rotations appear to be kinematically related to shear across a tear fault within the foreland fold and thrust belt of the colliding Finisterre Are, which in turn is aligned with and may be slructurally controlled by a major fault in the lower plate. These data indicate that vertical-axis rotations occurred during thrusting; consequently, the actual rotation rate is likely several times higher than the calculated minimum rate. Such very rapid rotations during thrust sheet eraplacement may be

ed lineations that differ markedly in azimuth in the three thrust sheets. The susceptibility lineations are rendered parallel by the same bedding-perpendicular rotations used to restore the palcomagnetic remanence to N-S thus independently confirming the rapid rotations. The restored lineations are perpendicular to the direction of tectonic transport, and the minimum susceptibility axes are slxeaked perpendicular to the lineation. We interpret these anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility data as primary sedimentary fabrics modified by weak strain accompanying foreland thrusting.
