section_candidates.excerpt: ES 537-550, JUNE 1997 Palcomagnetic evidence for rapid vertical-axis rotations during thrusting in an active collision zone, northeastern Papua New Guinea Peter D. Weiler and Robert S. Coe Department of Earth Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of three thrust sheets of the fold and thrust belt north of the Ramu-Markham Fault Zone (RMFZ) indicates very rapid vertical-axis rotations, with differential declination anomalies related to tectonic transport of thrust units. Data from this investigation indicate depositional ages straddling the Brun_hes-Matuyama reversal (780 ka) for the Leron Formation in Erap Valley. Net counterclockwise, vertical-axis rotations as great as 90 ø since 1 Ma have occurred locally in the Erap Valley area. These rotations appear to be kinematically related to shear across a tear fault within the foreland fold and thrust belt of the colliding Finisterre Are, which in turn is aligned with and may be slructurally controlled by a major fault in the lower plate. These data indicate that vertical-axis rotations occurred during thrusting; consequently, the actual rotation rate is likely several times higher than the calculated minimum rate. Such very rapid rotations during thrust sheet eraplacement may be

ed lineations that differ markedly in azimuth in the three thrust sheets. The susceptibility lineations are rendered parallel by the same bedding-perpendicular rotations used to restore the palcomagnetic remanence to N-S thus independently confirming the rapid rotations. The restored lineations are perpendicular to the direction of tectonic transport, and the minimum susceptibility axes are slxeaked perpendicular to the lineation. We interpret these anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility data as primary sedimentary fabrics modified by weak strain accompanying foreland thrusting. The important section at Escorihuela is sepa- rated from those in the Orrios, Villalba Alta area by 5 km. This sequence proved to be strongly magnetized and yielded excellent results in the basal two thirds of the section. The samples often unblocked at very high temperature (680°C), indi- cating the presence of hematite as the dominant magnetic carrier. The bottom 35 m of the section is reversely magnetized and the remainder of the section is of normal polarity, with the exception of the top site which is interpreted as having reversed polarity. Two fossil localities are located in this section; the stratigraphically lowest site (Escorihuela B) is MN 15 zone, in sediments that are reversely magnetized. The upper locality (Escorihuela A) (MN 16) is in sediments of normal polarity near the base of magnetozone Nt. We therefore correlate the R1-N1 transition in this sequence to the Gilbert/Gauss boundary. The mag- netic stratigraphy of these sectio

ere determined after analysis of orthogonal plots which allowed the determination of the various components of magnetization pre- sent in the samples. The direction of magnetization for each sample was determined by line fitting to the characteristic component of magnetization (Kirschvinck, 1980). A second high-temperature component, found in three other sample sites in the Hakl and in the Thumi areas, is probably a chemical remagnetization related to the emplacement of the upper ophiolite nappe in late Maastrichtian to Paleocene times. Finally a last high-temperature component, found only in the two sites from Naft area, could be a post-tectonic remagnetization acquired in Oligocene or Miocene times or represents differential tilting of pillows and sedimentary blocks. The high-temperature components are usually fairly scattered due to the very complex tectonic history of the area. Nevertheless, the relation between the defined paleopoles and the Indian polar wander is unambiguous and the evolution of the Masirah ophiolite from formation up to the emplacement of the second ophiolitic nappe is clearly related to the northward movement of the Indian plate. This new paleomagnetic study rules out the possibility of a common or related origin for the Masirah and the Semail ophiolites. 1. Paleomagnetic studies on ophiolites, predomi- nantly on the extrusive members and associated sedi- ments, are widely used for paleogeographic reloca- tion of ancient ocean floor fragments (e.g., Thomas et al., 1988; Perrin et al., 1994; Mubroto et al., 1994). The magnetic mineralogy of lava may un- dergo large alterations during seafloor and emplace- ment-related metamorphism. However, since sea- floor alteration takes place shortly after the extrusion of the lava, the first secondary ore mineral formation of magnetite or maghemite after Ti-magnetite will record the same field period (e.g., Pr~vot et al., 1979). Although the magnetic intensity is generally strongly reduced, the magnetization direction re- mains. An off-axis metamorphism in greenschist fa- cies may completely reset the magnetic signal to the prevailing magnetic field orientation. In the present study on lava from the lower Masirah ophiolitic nappe, we intend to support evi- dence for a complex structural evolution by paleo- magnetic methods and to reconstruct the origin of the lower Masirah nappe. Le M~tour et al. (1992) produced a 1:250,000 geological map of Masirah and described the folded Upper Cretaceous Fayah Formation from the island. Paleomagnetic studies on ophiolites, predomi- nantly on the extrusive members and associated sedi- ments, are widely used for paleogeographic reloca- tion of ancient ocean floor fragments (e.g., Thomas et al., 1988; Perrin et al., 1994; Mubroto et al., 1994). The magnetic mineralogy of lava may un- dergo large alterations during seafloor and emplace- ment-related metamorphism. However, since sea- floor alteration takes place shortly after the extrusion of the lava, the first secondary ore mineral formation of magnetite or maghemite after Ti-magnetite will record the same field period (e.g., Pr~vot et al., 1979). Although the magnetic intensity is generally strongly reduced, the magnetization direction re- mains. An off-axis metamorphism in greenschist fa- cies may completely reset the magnetic signal to the prevailing magnetic field orientation. In the present study on lava from the lower Masirah ophiolitic nappe, we intend to support evi- dence for a complex structural evolution by paleo- magnetic methods and to reconstruct the origin of the lower Masirah nappe. The magnetic mineralogy of lava may un- dergo large alterations during seafloor and emplace- ment-related metamorphism. However, since sea- floor alteration takes place shortly after the extrusion of the lava, the first secondary ore mineral formation of magnetite or maghemite after Ti-magnetite will record the same field period (e.g., Pr~vot et al., 1979). Although the magnetic intensity is generally strongly reduced, the magnetization direction re- mains. An off-axis metamorphism in greenschist fa- cies may completely reset the magnetic signal to the prevailing magnetic field orientation. In the present study on lava from the lower Masirah ophiolitic nappe, we intend to support evi- dence for a complex structural evolution by paleo- magnetic methods and to reconstruct the origin of the lower Masirah nappe. This study is a contribution to the Masirah project led by Prof. Peters, Universit

Sampling and mineralogy Eighty-four volcanic samples (Table 1) were taken in the well-exposed sheet flows and pillow and tube lavas from the top of the lower nappe with a water- cooled drill and oriented using both sun and mag- netic compasses. The sample sites are located in Fig. 1 (sample 72 was lost at the outcrop). The sampled lavas are predominantly tholeiitic (Abbotts, 1981), aphyric, or contain plagioclase phenocrysts. A second high-temperature component, found in three other sample sites in the Hakl and in the Thumi areas, is probably a chemical remagnetization related to the emplacement of the upper ophiolite nappe in late Maastrichtian to Paleocene times. Finally a last high-temperature component, found only in the two sites from Naft area, could be a post-tectonic remagnetization acquired in Oligocene or Miocene times or represents differential tilting of pillows and sedimentary blocks. Paleomagnetic studies on ophiolites, predomi- nantly on the extrusive members and associated sedi- ments, are widely used for paleogeographic reloca- tion of ancient ocean floor fragments (e.g., Thomas et al., 1988; Perrin et al., 1994; Mubroto et al., 1994). The magnetic mineralogy of lava may un- dergo large alterations during seafloor and emplace- ment-related metamorphism. However, since sea- floor alteration takes place shortly after the extrusion of the lava, the first secondary ore mineral formation of magnetite or maghemite after Ti-magnetite will record the same field period (e.g., Pr~vot et al., 1979). Although the magnetic intensity is generally strongly reduced, the magnetization direction re- mains. An off-axis metamorphism in greenschist fa- cies may completely reset the magnetic signal to the prevailing magnetic field orientation. In the present study on lava from the lower Masirah ophiolitic nappe, we intend to support evi- dence for a complex structural evolution by paleo- magnetic methods and to reconstruct the origin of the lower Masirah nappe. This study is a contribution to the Masirah project led by Prof. Peters, Universit

The sample sites are located in Fig. 1 (sample 72 was lost at the outcrop). The sampled lavas are predominantly tholeiitic (Abbotts, 1981), aphyric, or contain plagioclase phenocrysts. Bruere (Received December 15, 1992; revised version accepted July 12, 1993) Abstract The volcanic units of the Oman ophiolite were paleomagnetically studied in order to better constrain the large rotation of the nappe during emplacement suggested by previous paleomagnetic results. The volcanic sequence, going from pillow basalts extruded at the mid-oceanic ridge up to submarine lavas extruded during the oceanic thrusting, before the end of the abduction, displays components of magnetization which were acquired at various stages during the movement of the nappe on the sea floor. Paleomagnetic Euler Pole analysis shows that the movement can be modeled by a single, large rotation of about 145-150” around an Euler pole located close to the nappe (less than 200 km away). Bruere (Received December 15, 1992; revised version accepted July 12, 1993) Abstract The volcanic units of the Oman ophiolite were paleomagnetically studied in order to better constrain the large rotation of the nappe during emplacement suggested by previous paleomagnetic results. The volcanic sequence, going from pillow basalts extruded at the mid-oceanic ridge up to submarine lavas extruded during the oceanic thrusting, before the end of the abduction, displays components of magnetization which were acquired at various stages during the movement of the nappe on the sea floor. Paleomagnetic Euler Pole analysis shows that the movement can be modeled by a single, large rotation of about 145-150” around an Euler pole located close to the nappe (less than 200 km away). Combining plate tectonic concepts, a mantle-anchored hotspot reference frame and paleomagnetic data, we were able to determine the initial paleola

ction The Oman nappe is the largest ophiol~tic com- plex known in the world, with a crescent-shaped extension of over 500 km in length and 50-100 km in width. The ophiolitic nappe itself is divided into structural massifs, each several tens of kilo- meters long (Fig. 1). The nappe was abducted on the Arabian platform at the end of the Creta- ceous. It has not been disturbed by any subse- quent collision but it underwent a slight tilt dur- ing a post-Cretaceous tectonic event. For this reason, the ophiolitic section is complete, from the metamorphic sole resting on sedimentary nappes, through peridotites, gabbros and the sheeted dike complex, to the volcanic units in- terbedded with pelagic oceanic sediments. It is one of the best studied ophiolitic complex and many special volumes have been published (“Oman ophiolites”, J. Geophys. Res., vol. 86, 1981; “The ophiolites of Northern Oman”, Geol. Sot. Mem., vol. 11, 1986; “The ophiolite of Oman”, Tectonophysics, vol. 151, 1988). Prevot, F. Bruere (Received December 15, 1992; revised version accepted July 12, 1993) Abstract The volcanic units of the Oman ophiolite were paleomagnetically studied in order to better constrain the large rotation of the nappe during emplacement suggested by previous paleomagnetic results. The volcanic sequence, going from pillow basalts extruded at the mid-oceanic ridge up to submarine lavas extruded during the oceanic thrusting, before the end of the abduction, displays components of magnetization which were acquired at various stages during the movement of the nappe on the sea floor. Paleomagnetic Euler Pole analysis shows that the movement can be modeled by a single, large rotation of about 145-150” around an Euler pole located close to the nappe (less than 200 km away). Combining plate tectonic concepts, a mantle-anchored hotspot reference frame and paleomagnetic data, we were able to determine the initial paleola

ction The Oman nappe is the largest ophiol~tic com- plex known in the world, with a crescent-shaped extension of over 500 km in length and 50-100 km in width. The ophiolitic nappe itself is divided into structural massifs, each several tens of kilo- meters long (Fig. 1). The nappe was abducted on the Arabian platform at the end of the Creta- ceous. It has not been disturbed by any subse- quent collision but it underwent a slight tilt dur- ing a post-Cretaceous tectonic event. For this reason, the ophiolitic section is complete, from the metamorphic sole resting on sedimentary nappes, through peridotites, gabbros and the sheeted dike complex, to the volcanic units in- terbedded with pelagic oceanic sediments. It is one of the best studied ophiolitic complex and many special volumes have been published (“Oman ophiolites”, J. Geophys. Res., vol. 86, 1981; “The ophiolites of Northern Oman”, Geol. Sot. Mem., vol. 11, 1986; “The ophiolite of Oman”, Tectonophysics, vol. 151, 1988). Piper (1975) sampled the red sandstones and shales of the Fish River Subgroup and treated them with alternating field (AF) demagnetization. (1980) in labelling the various components for ease of comparison. Individual site means are listed in Table 2 along with the location of the site, formation and pertinent palaeomagnetic statistics. In general, low-temperature compo- nents in the red sediments refer to those components isolated at temperatures less than 500 "C, intermediate-temperature components refer to those isolated between 500 and 620°C and high-temperature components refer to those isolated at temperatures above 620 "C. Received 1997 January 28; in original form 1996 August 7 SUMMARY The Nama Group of southern Namibia is a candidate for the Terminal Proterozoic Global Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP). Desirable characteridics of a GSSP include a well-preserved index-fossil assemblage, little deformation or metamorphism, well-constrained isotopic ages, stable-isotope records and magnetostratigraphic control. The age of the Nama Group sediments is now constrained to between 570 and 510 Ma. Assuming the Gondwana assembly was nearly complete at this same time, there is a discrepancy between the previously published Nama poles, a revised 55CL510 Ma apparent polar wander path for Gondwana and the preceding supercontinental assemblages of Rodinia and Panottia. Individual site means are listed in Table 2 along with the location of the site, formation and pertinent palaeomagnetic statistics. The samples showed complex demagnetization direc- tions both within and between sites making it difficult to distinguish the sequence of remanence acquisition. The mag- netization in the limestones is most likely carried by magnetite, as indicated by the unblocking temperature, isothermal reman- ence acquisition (IRM) and Curie temperature experiments (Figs 5, 6, and 7). The magnetization in the red sediments is carried by both magnetite and haematite, as indicated by unblocking-temperature, IRM and Curie temperature experi- ments (Figs 5, 6 and 7). Desirable characteridics of a GSSP include a well-preserved index-fossil assemblage, little deformation or metamorphism, well-constrained isotopic ages, stable-isotope records and magnetostratigraphic control. s, the Nama Group sediments were resampled in an effort to evaluate the potential of detailing the magnetostratigra- phy of the Nama Group and resolving the discrepancy between the Nama poles and the APWP of Gondwana. Collectively, both the previous studies of the Nama Group and this one show a complex series of overprints and no easily discernible primary direction of magnetization. INTRODUCTION The assembly of the Gondwanan continent during the latest Proterozoic or earliest Palaeozoic followed the break-up of an earlier supercontinent, Rodinia (Fig. la; Dalziel 1992). The transition from Rodinia to Gondwana may have also included the formation of a short-lived supercontinent Panottia (Fig. lb) just prior to the opening of the Iapetus Ocean (Powell 1995). Siberia moved northwards during the Cambrian by about 10" of latitude. This movement was accompanied by anticlockwise rotation of about 30". A detailed biostratigraphic description of these exposures has been made by Rozanov et al. (1992) and Zinchenko, Vasilieva & Rudavskaya (1993). One of the most complete sequences of the Lower and Middle Cambrian is exposed along the middle and lower course of the Olenek River (Fig. 1). The Lower Cambrian platform deposits [up to the bottom of the Atdabanian stage (Zinchenko et al. 1993)] are represented in these outcrops by the Kessyusa Formation and by the lower part of the Erkeket Formation. The sediments of the Kessyusa Formation overlie the light-coloured dolomites of the Turkut Formation, the boundary being a stratigraphic unconformity. These Turkut dolomites contain a monotonous complex of stromatolites and microfitolites (Meshkova, Juravleva & Luchinina 1973; Savitsky et al. 1972). This complex, according to Rozanov et al. (1992) and Zinchenko et al. (1993), suggests a Vendian age for the Turkut Formation. The Kessyusa Formation is divided into three subformations (Vodanyuk & Karlova 1988; Rudavskaya & Vasilieva 1985). (1992) and Zinchenko et al. (1993), suggests a Vendian age for the Turkut Formation. The Kessyusa Formation is divided into three subformations (Vodanyuk & Karlova 1988; Rudavskaya & Vasilieva 1985). The lower subformation consists of three parts: the lower part is composed of sandstones, the middle part is composed of siltstones and the upper part is represented by terrigenous and carbonaceous deposits. The middle subformation is represented mainly by monotonous dark argillaceous sediments. The highly variable upper subformation consists of three parts: the lower part comprises siltstones and sandstones, the middle part is carbonaceous and the upper part is represented by carbon- aceous and terrigenous sediments. The whole thickness of the Kessyusa Formation varies from 100 to 110 m. There are several opinions as to the age of the Kessyusa Formation. According to Rozanov et al. (1992) only the upper subformation belongs to the Lower Cambrian (Tommotian stage), and the two lower subformations are of Vendian age (Nemakit-Daldynian regional stage). However, a number of other researchers (e.g. Zinchenko et al. 1993) have suggested an Early Cambrian age for the whole Kessyusa Formation based on the occurrence of acritarchs. Vidal, Moczydlowska & Rudavskaya (1995) confirmed an Early Cambrian age for the upper subformation of the Kessyusa Formation. They reported similar acritarch assemblages in the Tommotian stage. There are three K-Ar dates from outcrop 13 (Fig. 1) (Nikolaeva, Zagruzina & Murina 1986), but their range is very large: 461, 505 and 593 Ma.
